# Introduction

In this project we will explore the Bible, specifically King James Bible.
The main goal is to train a model, that would take an arbitrary verse from the King James Bible and classify it into either Old or New Testament.
This would help us understand the differences between the two Testaments on a textual level and help us answer the question: "What are the main words that differentiate the Old and New Testament?".

In this report you can find the whole process of data exploration, analysis and modeling.
In data section we will introduce the dataset in more detail and perform a data quality check.
Then, we will do some in depth data analysis to understand the structure and distribution of the data, both on a textual and verse level.
Finally, we will train a classification model, evaluate its performance and look at the most important features.

We will be dealing mainly with text data, thus some text preprocessing will be needed.
We will be using Python programming language with libraries such as Pandas, Seaborn, Matplotlib and Scikit-learn for data manipulation, visualization and modeling.

## Planned Steps

Firstly we will load and parse the data.
Then we will perform a data quality check to ensure that the dataset is complete and does not contain any duplicates or missing values.
Next, we will clean the text data by removing punctuation and converting everything to lowercase.
After that we will do some analysis of the data.
This will include looking at the distribution of verses per book and chapter, as well as some word based analysis of the text.
We will also experiment with filtering out stopwords to see how it affects the analysis.
Finally, we will train a classification model using TF-IDF vectorization and Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm.

Another options for the modeling part could be to use other algorithms such as Logistic Regression, Random Forest or even some of the deep learning models.
For the text vectorization part we could also experiment with other techniques such as Count Vectorization or Word Embeddings (e.g. Word2Vec, GloVe).
But for the sake of simplicity and interpretability we will stick with TF-IDF and SVM (as it outputted the best results in our experiments).

# Data

This section introduces the King James Bible dataset and performs a data quality check to ensure that the dataset is complete and ready for further analysis.

The King James Bible dataset contains full text of the Bible divided into verses.
The dataset have been provided by our teachers[1] in a simple text format with non-standard delimiters.
The format (columns) of the dataset is the following: `Book Chapter:Verse    Text`, where:

:::{.column-margin}
\[1\]: [https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/](https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/)
:::

- Book - name of the book where the verse can be found
- Chapter - chapter number
- Verse - verse number
- Text - text of the verse

Thus, after loading and parsing the data we have the following dataframe structure:

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Sample
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

bible_df = pd.read_csv(
    "../data/bible.txt",
    sep="\t",
    header=None,
    names=["ref", "text"],
    engine="python",
)
parts = bible_df["ref"].str.extract(
    r"^(?P<book>.+?)\s+(?P<chapter>\d+):(?P<verse>\d+)$"
)

bible_df = pd.concat([parts, bible_df["text"]], axis=1)

types = {
    "book": "string",
    "chapter": "int32",
    "verse": "int32",
    "text": "string",
}
bible_df = bible_df.astype(types)

bible_df.head()
```

## Types

```{python}
bible_df.dtypes
```
:::

Data seems to be loaded correctly are at first glance seems to be correct.
But just to be sure we will do checks later on.
For completeness, under the Types tab we can see the data types of each column, that are as we would expect them to be.

## Data Check

In this sub-section we will perform a data quality check to ensure that our dataset is ready for further analysis.
Firstly, let's look if we have correct numbers of books, chapters and verses.

```{python}
print(f"Total number of lines (verses): {len(bible_df)}")
print(f"Number of duplicate lines: {bible_df.duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"Number of unique books: {bible_df['book'].nunique()}")
print(f"Number of chapters: {bible_df.groupby(['book', 'chapter']).ngroups}")
```

As we can see, there are no duplicate lines in the dataset.
On web \[[2](https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts)\]\[[3](https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics)\] we managed to find the following statistics about the King James Bible:

:::{.column-margin}
\[2\]: [https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts](https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts)

\[3\]: [https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics](https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics)
:::

- 66 books,
- 1,189 chapters,
- 31,102 verses.

These numbers match exactly with numbers obtained from our dataset.
Next, let's check for missing values:

```{python}
print(f"Number of missing values:\n{bible_df.isna().sum()}")
```

Luckily, there are no missing values in the dataset.

Now let's check for any potential duplicates.
We will check both duplicate records (book+chapter+verse+text) and duplicate verses (text).

```{python}
print(f"Number of duplicate records: {bible_df.duplicated().sum()}")
duplicated_verses = bible_df[bible_df.duplicated(subset=['text'])]
print(f"Number of duplicate verses: {duplicated_verses.shape[0]}")
```

This might seem concerning at first, but after looking at some of the duplicate verses we can see that they are indeed the same verses appearing in different books/chapters.

## Preprocessing and Cleaning

Before we can proceed with the analysis, we need to do some preprocessing and cleaning of the text data.
For the analysis part we will need to clean the text by removing punctuation and converting everything to lowercase.
This will help us in the word based analysis later on.

Another thing we need to do is to create a new column indicating the Testament (Old or New) for each verse.
Let's now look, how the data looks after these preprocessing steps.

```{python}
def assign_testament(book):
    old_testament_books = [
        # Historical books
        "Genesis", "Exodus", "Leviticus", "Numbers", "Deuteronomy", "Joshua", "Judges", "Ruth", "1 Samuel", "2 Samuel", "1 Kings", "2 Kings", "1 Chronicles", "2 Chronicles", "Ezra", "Nehemiah", "Esther",
        # Poetic books
        "Job", "Psalms", "Proverbs", "Ecclesiastes", "Song of Solomon",
        # Prophetic books
        "Isaiah", "Jeremiah", "Lamentations", "Ezekiel", "Daniel", "Hosea", "Joel", "Amos", "Obadiah", "Jonah", "Micah", "Nahum", "Habakkuk", "Zephaniah", "Haggai", "Zechariah", "Malachi"
    ]

    new_testament_books = [
        # Gospels:
        "Matthew", "Mark", "Luke", "John",
        # Historical:
        "Acts",
        # Epistles:
        "Romans", "1 Corinthians", "2 Corinthians", "Galatians", "Ephesians", "Philippians", "Colossians", "1 Thessalonians", "2 Thessalonians", "1 Timothy", "2 Timothy", "Titus", "Philemon", "Hebrews", "James", "1 Peter", "2 Peter", "1 John", "2 John", "3 John", "Jude",
        # The Revelation:
        "Revelation"
    ]

    if book in old_testament_books:
        return "Old"
    elif book in new_testament_books:
        return "New"
    else:
        return "Unknown"

bible_df["testament"] = bible_df["book"].apply(assign_testament)

import re

def clean_text(text):
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", " ", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text

bible_df["cleaned_text"] = bible_df["text"].apply(clean_text)
bible_df.head()
```

The way Testaments are assigned also adds possibility to check if there are any unknown books in the dataset.
From the previous check we know that the number of books is correct, but we haven't checked if all the books really are books from the Bible.

```{python}
print(f"Unknown testaments present: {(bible_df['testament'] == 'Unknown').sum()}")
```

No verse is assigned to "Unknown" testament, thus we can be sure that all books in the dataset are indeed from the Bible.

This concludes the 'Data' section.
We have successfully loaded, parsed and cleaned the dataset and so we can proceed to the analysis part.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

In this section we will perform some exploratory data analysis (EDA) to understand the structure and distribution of the data.
Firstly, we are going to look at the distribution of verses, and then we will look at word based comparisons of Testaments.
At the end we will summarize the findings from the analysis and point out what can we expect from the model and what we should be cautious about.

## Verse distribution

Let's plot the distribution of verses per book divided into chapters.

:::{.panel-tabset}

```{python}
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 12))
sns.histplot(

    legend=False,
)
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
```

## Data

```{python}
book_stats = bible_df.groupby("book").agg(
    num_chapters=("chapter", "nunique"),
    num_verses=("verse", "count"),
).reset_index()
book_stats
```

:::

As we can see from the histogram above, some books have significantly more verses than others.
The average number of the verses per book, maximum and minimum number of verses per book are the following:

```{python}
book_lengths = bible_df.groupby('book').size()
book_lengths_old = bible_df[bible_df['testament'] == 'Old'].groupby('book').size()
book_lengths_new = bible_df[bible_df['testament'] == 'New'].groupby('book').size()
print(f"Average number of verses per book: {book_lengths.mean():.2f} (std: {book_lengths.std():.2f})")
print(f"Longest book(old): {book_lengths_old.idxmax()} ({book_lengths_old.max()} verses)")
print(f"Longest book(new): {book_lengths_new.idxmax()} ({book_lengths_new.max()} verses)")
print(f"Shortest book(old): {book_lengths_old.idxmin()} ({book_lengths_old.min()} verses)")
print(f"Shortest book(new): {book_lengths_new.idxmin()} ({book_lengths_new.min()} verses)")
```

We can see that there is quite a big variance in the number of verses per book.
The longest book (Psalms) belongs to the Old Testament and is more than twice as long as the longest book in the New Testament (Luke).
Similar trend can be observed for the shortest books as well.
The shortest book in the Old Testament (Obadiah) nearly has twice as many verses as the shortest book in the New Testament (2 John).

Another thing that can be observed from the histogram above is that first half of the dataset (that corresponds to Old Testament), is not only longer by the number of books, but also by the number of verses per book.
The of number of verses per Testament is captured in the following chart.

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Plot
```{python}
import numpy as np

def label_percentage(pct, allvals):
    absolute = int(pct / 100. * np.sum(allvals))
    return f"{pct:.1f}%\n({absolute:d} verses)"

# piechart of number of verses per Testament
verse_counts = bible_df['testament'].value_counts()
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

plt.pie(
    verse_counts.values,
    labels=verse_counts.index,
    autopct=lambda pct: label_percentage(pct, verse_counts.values),
    startangle=140,
    colors=sns.color_palette("pastel")
)
plt.title("Relative number of verses per Testament")
plt.show()
```
## Data
```{python}
print("Number of verses per Testament:")
print(verse_counts)
```
:::

As we can see, the Old Testament is nearly three times larger then the New Testament in terms of number of verses.
Since we are going to classify the verses, we can expect class imbalance issues in the model.
We should be cautious about accuracy metric as it can be misleading in imbalanced datasets.
Another thing to look out for is making sure that there is enough representation of the smaller class (New Testament) in both training and test sets.
This can be achieved by stratified sampling during the train-test split.

## Word based analysis

In this sub-section we will perform some word based analysis of the two Testaments.
Firstly we will introduce the concept of stopwords, then we will look at word verses analysis, vocabulary overlap and finally most used words in the Bible.

### Stopwords

Before we start, we should mention the concept of **stopwords**.
If we look at text, not all words carry significant meaning (e.g. "the", "and", "of", etc.).
These are called stopwords and usually it makes sense to filter them out before doing the analysis and modeling.
The list of stopwords that we will use here is again provided by our teachers[1].

```{python}
with open("../data/stopwords-big.txt", "r") as f:
    stopwords = set(f.read().splitlines())

print(f"Number of stopwords: {len(stopwords)}")
print("Some stopwords:", list(stopwords)[:10])
```

This is pretty rich set of stopwords.
Most of the analysis will be done both with and without stopwords to see how it affects the results.
This will help us decide whether to use stopwords filtering in the modeling part or not.

### Word verses analysis

Now let's look at sizes of verses in terms of number of words.
The sizes of verses are important as they determine the context size that the model will have to work with.

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Plot
```{python}
# Unfiltered averages (with stopwords)
avg_words_per_verse = bible_df.groupby('testament')['cleaned_text'].apply(
    lambda x: x.str.split().apply(len).mean()
)

# Filtered averages (without stopwords)
def count_non_stopwords(s):
    return sum(1 for w in s.split() if w not in stopwords)

filtered_avg_words_per_verse = bible_df.groupby('testament')['cleaned_text'].apply(
    lambda x: x.apply(count_non_stopwords).mean()
)

# Combine into a single dataframe for plotting
avg_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Testament': list(avg_words_per_verse.index) + list(filtered_avg_words_per_verse.index),
    'AverageWords': list(avg_words_per_verse.values) + list(filtered_avg_words_per_verse.values),
    'Type': ['Unfiltered'] * len(avg_words_per_verse) + ['Filtered'] * len(filtered_avg_words_per_verse)
})

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
sns.barplot(data=avg_df, x='Testament', y='AverageWords', hue='Type', palette="pastel")
plt.title("Average number of words per verse per Testament")
plt.xlabel("Testament")
plt.ylabel("Average number of words per verse")
# Whole-Bible constant lines (guide)
overall_unfiltered_avg = bible_df['cleaned_text'].str.split().apply(len).mean()
overall_filtered_avg = bible_df['cleaned_text'].apply(count_non_stopwords).mean()

line1 = plt.axhline(overall_unfiltered_avg, color='gray', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='Overall (Unfiltered)')
line2 = plt.axhline(overall_filtered_avg, color='gray', linestyle=':', linewidth=1.5, label='Overall (Filtered)')

# Combine legend entries for bars and lines
ax = plt.gca()
handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
plt.legend(handles=handles, labels=labels, title='Text + Overall')
plt.show()
```
## Data
```{python}
print("Average number of words per verse per Testament:")
print(avg_words_per_verse)
print("\nAverage number of words per verse per Testament (filtered):")
print(filtered_avg_words_per_verse)
print("\nOverall average words per verse (unfiltered):", overall_unfiltered_avg)
print("Overall average words per verse (filtered):", overall_filtered_avg)
```
:::

We can see that the lengths of verses in the Old Testament are generally slightly longer than those in the New Testament.
This trend holds both for unfiltered and filtered text.
This might be caused by the fact that Old Testament contains more historical and poetic books, which tend to have longer verses.
Another possibility is that there is used more archaic language in the Old Testament, which might lead to longer verses.

The same trend can be observed when looking at the average number of words per verse with stopwords filtered out.
We can see that filtering out the stopwords significantly reduces the average number of words per verse (nearly 3 times).
But still we have to remember that those words that stay are the meaningful ones, thus the context size for the model is still quite decent.

Let's now look at the extremes - longest and shortest verses (with and without stopwords).

```{python}
def longest_verse(df, testament_name, stopwords = []):
    new_df = df.copy()
    new_df['word_count'] = new_df['cleaned_text'].apply(lambda x: len([word for word in x.split() if word not in stopwords]))
    longest_verse = new_df.loc[new_df['word_count'].idxmax()]
    print(f"Longest verse in {testament_name}: {longest_verse['book']} {longest_verse['chapter']}:{longest_verse['verse']} ({longest_verse['word_count']} words)")

def shortest_verse(df, testament_name, stopwords = []):
    new_df = df.copy()
    new_df['word_count'] = new_df['cleaned_text'].apply(lambda x: len([word for word in x.split() if word not in stopwords]))
    shortest_verse = new_df.loc[new_df['word_count'].idxmin()]
    print(f"Shortest verse in {testament_name}: {shortest_verse['book']} {shortest_verse['chapter']}:{shortest_verse['verse']} ({shortest_verse['word_count']} words)")

old_testament_df = bible_df[bible_df["testament"] == "Old"]
new_testament_df = bible_df[bible_df["testament"] == "New"]

print("Without stopwords filtered out:")
longest_verse(old_testament_df, "Old Testament")
longest_verse(new_testament_df, "New Testament")
shortest_verse(old_testament_df, "Old Testament")
shortest_verse(new_testament_df, "New Testament")
print("\nWith stopwords filtered out:")
longest_verse(old_testament_df, "Old Testament", stopwords=stopwords)
longest_verse(new_testament_df, "New Testament", stopwords=stopwords)
shortest_verse(old_testament_df, "Old Testament", stopwords=stopwords)
shortest_verse(new_testament_df, "New Testament", stopwords=stopwords)
```

Main observation from the above is that the shortest verse in New Testament, when filtered for stopwords, has 0 words.
This means that the verse contains only stopwords.
This can indicate that our *set of stopwords is too restrictive* and might cause problems later, as we would also like to classify such verses correctly.

### Vocabulary

Another interesting analysis is to look at the vocabulary and the overlap between the two Testaments.

<!--
Venn diagrams of vocabulary overlap between Old and New Testament
-->
:::{.panel-tabset}

## Plot
```{python}
from matplotlib_venn import venn2

# Unfiltered vocabulary
old_words = set(
    ' '.join(bible_df[bible_df['testament'] == 'Old']['cleaned_text']).split()
)
new_words = set(
    ' '.join(bible_df[bible_df['testament'] == 'New']['cleaned_text']).split()
)

# Filtered vocabulary (without stopwords)
old_words_filtered = old_words - stopwords
new_words_filtered = new_words - stopwords

# Create side-by-side Venn diagrams
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 7))

# Unfiltered
plt.sca(ax1)
venn2(
    subsets = (len(old_words - new_words), len(new_words - old_words), len(old_words & new_words)),
    set_labels = ('Old Testament', 'New Testament'),
    set_colors = ('#ff9999','#66b3ff'),
    alpha = 0.7
)
ax1.set_title("Vocabulary overlap (Unfiltered)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

# Filtered
plt.sca(ax2)
venn2(
    subsets = (len(old_words_filtered - new_words_filtered), len(new_words_filtered - old_words_filtered), len(old_words_filtered & new_words_filtered)),
    set_labels = ('Old Testament', 'New Testament'),
    set_colors = ('#ff9999','#66b3ff'),
    alpha = 0.7
)
ax2.set_title("Vocabulary overlap (Filtered)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Data
```{python}
print("Unfiltered vocabulary:")
print(f"  Number of unique words in Old Testament: {len(old_words)}")
print(f"  Number of unique words in New Testament: {len(new_words)}")
print(f"  Number of common words: {len(old_words & new_words)}")

print("\nFiltered vocabulary (stopwords removed):")
print(f"  Number of unique words in Old Testament: {len(old_words_filtered)}")
print(f"  Number of unique words in New Testament: {len(new_words_filtered)}")
print(f"  Number of common words: {len(old_words_filtered & new_words_filtered)}")
```
:::

From the Venn diagrams above we can observe that there is huge imbalance in vocabulary size between the two Testaments, especially in the vocabulary that is unique to the Old Testament.
The old Testament has three time more unique words than the New Testament and nearly two times more words in total.
This can again cause problems for the model as it will have harder time classifying verses from the smaller class (New Testament) due to lack of vocabulary coverage.

This also shows that there is not a significant difference when filtering out the stopwords.
Actually we can see that the largest difference is in the common vocabulary.
This would actually help the model as it would have less common words to confuse the two Testaments.

### Most used words

Finally, let's look at the most common words in the Bible.
Again, we will look at both unfiltered and filtered (without stopwords) versions.
Firstly, the unfiltered version.

<!--
Top 20 most common words in the Bible
-->
:::{.panel-tabset}
## Plot
```{python}
def plot_top_words(df, testament_name, number_of_words=20, stopwords=[]):
    words = pd.Series(
        ' '.join(df['cleaned_text']).split()
    )
    if stopwords:
        words = words[~words.isin(stopwords)]
    top_words = words.value_counts().head(number_of_words)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.barplot(
        x=top_words.index,
        y=top_words.values,
        palette="viridis"
    )
    plt.xticks(rotation=90)
    plt.title(f"Top 20 most common words in {testament_name}")
    plt.xlabel("Words")
    plt.ylabel("Frequency")
    plt.show()
    return top_words

top_words_bible = plot_top_words(bible_df, "Bible")
```
## Data
```{python}
print("Top 20 most common words in Bible")
print(top_words_bible)
```
:::

We can see that the most common words are mostly stopwords.
Actually, the only word that is not a stopword is "lord".
This is surprising, as we would expect more meaningful words to be among the most common ones.

Let's remove the stopwords and look at the most common words again.

<!--
Top 20 most common words in the Bible (filtered)
-->
:::{.panel-tabset}
## Plot
```{python}
top_words_bible_filtered = plot_top_words(bible_df, "Bible", stopwords=stopwords)
```
## Data
```{python}
print("Top 20 most common words in Bible (filtered)")
print(top_words_bible_filtered)
```
:::

As expected, after filtering out the stopwords, we can see more meaningful words.
Still, there are some words that could be considered stopwords (e.g. "thou", "thy").
These are archaic words that are not commonly used in modern English, but they might still be used in the Bible.
This also suggests that the set of stopwords could be further improved for our specific use case.

We can also see that most of the words are related to religious context (e.g. "god", "lord", "son", "israel", etc.).
This is expected from the nature of the text of choice.

## Summary of findings

From the exploratory data analysis we can summarize the following findings:

- There is significant class imbalance between the two Testaments, with Old Testament being nearly three times larger than New Testament in terms of number of verses. This implies that we should be cautious about accuracy metric and ensure stratified sampling during train-test split.
- The lengths of verses in the Old Testament are generally slightly longer than those in the New Testament.
- There is huge imbalance in vocabulary size between the two Testaments, especially in the vocabulary that is unique to the Old Testament.
- Both the last two points again suggest that the model might have harder time classifying verses from the smaller class (New Testament) due to lack of vocabulary coverage and shorter context size.
- The set of stopwords at hand seems to be not adequate for our specific use case, as some verses contain only stopwords and some archaic stopwords are not included in the set.

We should keep these findings in mind when proceeding to the modeling part.

# Modeling

In this section we will train a classification model to classify verses into Old and New Testament.
Later we will evaluate the model performance and look at the most important features.

## Model description

For the modeling part we will be using TF-IDF vectorization for text representation and Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm for classification.

The only preprocessing step that remains is to split the data into training and test sets using stratified sampling to ensure that both sets have similar class distribution.
For that we will use the split function from Scikit-learn library.
The test size is set to be 20% of the whole dataset.

We will use TF-IDF vectorizer with both unigrams and bigrams, minimum document frequency of 3 and maximum number of features set to 50,000.
We will not filter out any stopwords for the modeling part, as we have seen in the analysis part that some verses contain only stopwords.

The classification algorithm will be Linear Support Vector Classifier (LinearSVC) with maximum number of iterations set to 2000.

## Evaluation

Let's now train the model and evaluate its performance using cross-validation on the training set and then on the test set.

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, accuracy_score, f1_score

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    bible_df["cleaned_text"],
    bible_df["testament"],
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=bible_df["testament"],
    random_state=42
)

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(
    ngram_range=(1,2),
    analyzer="word",
    min_df=3,
    max_features=50000,
    stop_words=None
)

X_train_tfidf = tfidf.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_tfidf  = tfidf.transform(X_test)

svc = LinearSVC(max_iter=2000, random_state=42, dual=False)

# Cross-validation on training set
print("Cross-validation scores (5-fold):")
cv_scores = cross_val_score(svc, X_train_tfidf, y_train, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
print(f"Accuracy: {cv_scores.mean():.4f} (+/- {cv_scores.std() * 2:.4f})")

cv_f1_scores = cross_val_score(svc, X_train_tfidf, y_train, cv=5, scoring='f1_macro')
print(f"F1 Score (macro): {cv_f1_scores.mean():.4f} (+/- {cv_f1_scores.std() * 2:.4f})")

# Train on full training set
svc.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)

# Evaluate on test set
pred = svc.predict(X_test_tfidf)
print("\nTest set performance:")
print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, pred))
print("F1 Score (macro):", f1_score(y_test, pred, average='macro'))
print("F1 Score (weighted):", f1_score(y_test, pred, average='weighted'))
print("\nDetailed classification report:")
print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
```

The model performs quite well on both cross-validation and test set.
The accuracy is at 94.5%.
As mentioned before, accuracy can be misleading in imbalanced datasets, thus we also look at F1 scores.
The macro F1 score is at 0.926 on the test set, which is also quite good.
Let's now look at the confusion matrix to see where the model makes mistakes.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

labels = svc.classes_

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred, labels=labels)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
cax = ax.imshow(cm, interpolation="nearest")
plt.title("Confusion Matrix")
plt.colorbar(cax)

ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(labels)))
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(labels)))
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set_yticklabels(labels)

# Print numbers on matrix
for i in range(len(labels)):
    for j in range(len(labels)):
        ax.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center")

plt.xlabel("Predicted")
plt.ylabel("Actual")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As predicted the model makes more mistakes classifying the verses from the New Testament.
The number if misclassified verses is not as high as we could expect.
More surprising might be that there is also a significant number of misclassified verses from the Old Testament.
It's just half as many as from the New Testament.
Considering the class imbalance (size of training set, vocabulary, verse lengths, etc.) one would expect better performance on the Old Testament verses.
On the other hand, this shows that the model is not biased towards the larger class, which is a good sign.

Next, let's look at ROC curve for the model.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, auc, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import label_binarize

# Convert labels to binary (Old = 1, New = 0)
y_bin = label_binarize(y_test, classes=["New", "Old"]).ravel()

# Get decision function scores (LinearSVC doesn't have predict_proba by default)
# Negate scores to align with class order (Old=0, New=1)
y_scores = svc.decision_function(X_test_tfidf)

# Calculate ROC curve
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_bin, y_scores)
roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)

# Plot ROC Curve
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, linewidth=2, label=f"AUC = {roc_auc:.3f}")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="gray")
plt.title("ROC Curve")
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

We can see that the ROC curve is close to the top-left corner, which indicates good performance (perfect ROC would pass through the top-left corner).
To translate this into a single number, we can look at the Area Under the Curve (AUC).
The AUC is 0.982, which is quite high and indicates that the model is able to distinguish between the two classes quite well.

Lastly, let's look at the Precision-Recall curve.

```{python}
# Calculate Precision-Recall curve
precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_bin, y_scores)
pr_auc = average_precision_score(y_bin, y_scores)

# Plot Precision-Recall Curve
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.plot(recall, precision, linewidth=2, label=f"AP = {pr_auc:.3f}")
plt.fill_between(recall, precision, alpha=0.2)
plt.title("Precision-Recall Curve")
plt.xlabel("Recall")
plt.ylabel("Precision")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.xlim([0, 1])
plt.ylim([0, 1])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The Precision-Recall curve also shows good performance, with high precision and recall values across different thresholds.
The Average Precision (AP) is 0.992, which is also quite high and indicates that the model is able to maintain high precision while achieving high recall.

##  Important features

Finally, we will be able to look at the most important features (words) that the model uses to distinguish between the two Testaments.

:::{.panel-tabset}
## Plot

```{python}
import numpy as np

feature_names = tfidf.get_feature_names_out()
coef = svc.coef_[0]

top_new = np.argsort(coef)[-20:]
top_old = np.argsort(coef)[:20]

top_features = np.concatenate([top_old, top_new])
top_values = coef[top_features]
top_labels = feature_names[top_features]

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
positions = np.arange(len(top_features))
plt.barh(positions, top_values)
plt.yticks(positions, top_labels)
plt.title("Top 15 Discriminative Words (Old vs New Testament)")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Data

```{python}
print("New Testament:")
for i in reversed(top_new):
    print(f"{feature_names[i]}: {coef[i]:.4f}")

print("\nOld Testament:")
for i in top_old:
    print(f"{feature_names[i]}: {coef[i]:.4f}")
```
:::

As we can see the top three words indicating New Testament are "jesus", "christ" and "faith".
This is expected as the New Testament focuses on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ and the establishment of Christianity.

On the other hand, the top three words indicating Old Testament are "lord", "the" and "israel".
Moreover, the feature containg "lord" is bigram containing also "the".
This is surprising as "the" is a stopword and we would not expect it to be among the most important features, let alone two times.

Another thing to point out is that the weights of the top words for the Old Testament are smaller than those for the New Testament.
This suggests that the model relies more heavily on specific words to identify New Testament verses, while Old Testament verses are identified by a broader range of words with smaller individual weights.
